title: The 1997–2004 Chevrolet Corvette (C5) Is Still a High-Performance Bargain

body_markdown:
Along the way in the development history of the Corvette, there have been several big milestones. The[1955](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chevrolet/corvette/1955/1955-chevrolet-corvette-base?id=aCn1I000000DHqFSAW) model introduced the small-block V-8. The C2 in[1963](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=1963+corvette) introduced independent rear suspension. The C4 marked a massive upgrade in Corvette handling, with an all-new chassis that replaced a design that had been largely unchanged since its introduction. The move to the fifth-generation (C5) Corvette, however, was a monumental shift in America’s sports car, the kind that we wouldn’t see again until the mid-engine move with the[2020 C8](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=2020+corvette) .


As Corvettes do, C5s became used cars in the late 2000s and 2010s, and depreciated. Prices for the very best examples have ticked up in recent years, but fifth gen Vettes are still some of the best performance values out there, whether it’s an automatic convertible for weekend cruising or a Z06 for track days.


Chevrolet


Introduced for 1997, the C5 featured an entirely new chassis with transverse leaf springs and upper and lower A-arms front and rear, replacing the multilink trailing arm design of the C4. Interestingly, the cast aluminum front and rear uprights on the C5 are identical, with the front left and right rear using the same casting, and the same is true of the front right and left rear.


Another major change, one that stuck with Corvette through the C6 and C7 generations, was the move to a rear-mounted transmission bolted directly to the rear differential. Indeed, the C5 set the blueprint for 23 years of Corvette production that expanded the trend the C4 started of offering world-class handling and exotic-level performance.


The C5-R showed off Corvette performance on the world stage. In the 55 races where the C5-R competed, it had 50 podiums and 31 wins. It delivered four team championships and four constructors’ championships, while taking class wins at Daytona, Sebring, and Le Mans.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


The 1997 Corvette also brought an entirely new iteration of the small-block V-8, the LS1, that shared nothing with its predecessor save for its roller lifters, rod bearings, and 4.4-inch bore spacing. The LS1 featured a cast-aluminum, deep-skirt block with cross-bolted main bearing caps that offered a rigid foundation. It bolted to a cast-aluminum oil pan that further tied the bottom end together. Weighing in at just over 100 pounds, the bare block was about a third lighter than its cast-iron, Gen II small-block predecessor. The block was topped with cast-aluminum heads with evenly spaced exhaust ports and tall, peaked intake ports that became known as “cathedral ports”.


Those new heads ditched the mirrored valve arrangement of the Gen I and Gen II Chevy small-block V-8, eliminating the hot spot in the head between the center two exhaust ports. While the Gen I and Gen II small-block had placed its valves at a 23-degree angle relative to the bore centerline, the Gen III rotated them to 15 degrees. It all added up to improved flow into and out of the engine. The heads were bridged by a low-profile, glass-reinforced nylon intake manifold, appropriate considering the Corvette’s glass-reinforced plastic body panels.


Thanks to fantastic cylinder heads, the LS1, like all other GM pushrod V-8s in the family that followed, offered great performance with very mild cam timing. Cam swaps can yield big power gains.


Chevrolet


GM’s goal for the LS1 was to create a lighter, more efficient V-8 that produced one horsepower per cubic inch. The 1997 LS1 that debuted in the first year of the C5 did almost exactly that, with a rating of 345 hp to go with its 346 cubic-inch displacement. The LS1 did eventually get a 350 hp rating with the addition of the LS6 intake manifold starting in 2001. Speaking of the LS6. . .


## C5 Corvette Variants


The C5 debuted with a single model, a targa-roof hatchback with a generous cargo area. A convertible joined the lineup for 1998, marking the first Corvette with a trunk since 1962. In 1999, a fixed-roof coupe (FRC) was added to offer a lower-cost entry point. It combined the convertible’s trunk and decklid with a fixed top over the coupe’s structural roof hoop. With the top permanently bonded to the windshield frame, the hardtop was more rigid. Without the large glass hatch, it was lighter too. Every 1999 FRC came equipped with a six-speed manual and the Z51 suspension for improved handling.[It remains the most affordable way to get into a C5](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chevrolet/corvette/2000/2000-chevrolet-corvette-base?id=aCn1I000000CybcSAC) .


The FRC was discontinued for 2001, sort of. The body style returned, but only in the guise of the new Z06, a return of the performance option package that famously gathered a host of road-race options for the 1963 Sting Ray.


Chevrolet


You can identify a Z06 by its 10-spoke wheels, wider tires, fender emblem, and its rear brake cooling ducts located just ahead of the wheel opening. A performance-tuned suspension and improved brakes were combined with the LS6 engine to round out the Z06 package. The same displacement as the LS1, the LS6 used new heads with improved flow and a smaller combustion chamber that increased the compression ratio to 10.5:1.


Paired with an improved intake—shared with the LS1s used in the Corvette and the F-body starting in 2001—and a new camshaft with a touch more lift and duration, the 2001 LS6 produced 385 hp.[In 2002](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chevrolet/corvette/2002/2002-chevrolet-corvette-z06?id=aCn1I000000DRbISAW) , Chevrolet gave the LS6 a new cam with even more lift and duration. The engine was just a bit rowdier, without any loss in low-rpm torque. The added power started to make itself known at about 3500 rpm, with a new peak of 405 hp. The Z06’s fender emblem reflected the change, with the horsepower number called out for the first time.


Hagerty Marketplace/Charles_Miele


C5 Corvettes have received praise from the motoring press ever since they launched, with particularly rave reviews for the driver-focused Z06. Enthusiasts have always known they offer surprising practicality with respectable fuel economy and great reliability. Their most well-known shortcoming is a rather lackluster interior, although that too was praised for being more comfortable to a wider range of drivers and passengers than its predecessor. In short, there’s a lot to love about the C5 Corvette, and it is still a driver favorite.


The 2003 Chevrolet Corvette 50th Anniversary Edition has held its value over the last five years, but its premium over the base model has narrowed.


Chevrolet


According to the demographics of Hagerty Members, the baby boomer crowd is still holding onto C5s. Boomers make up 34% of collector car buyers, but account for 47% of the C5 market. Millennial buyers are underrepresented by the largest margin, making up 21% of collectors overall but only 12% of C5 owners. These are buyers who are old enough to remember when the C5 hit the market, but are getting into the prime Corvette-buying time just as the mid-engine C8 is driving down the average age of a new Corvette buyer. Gen X and Gen Z are both slightly underrepresented in the C5 market, with the younger buyers actually favoring the more affordable C4 Corvette.


It seems that the stereotype of a low-mileage, garage-kept Corvette owned by an older driver is true, as Hagerty Senior Auction Editor Andrew Newton has pointed out a widening gap between the very[well-kept #2 (excellent) cars](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chevrolet/corvette/1997/1997-chevrolet-corvette-base?id=aCn1I000000DNdSSAW&condition=excellent) and the[average #3 (good) condition cars](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chevrolet/corvette/1997/1997-chevrolet-corvette-base?id=aCn1I000000DNdSSAW) . “ Five years ago, the median #3 value was $17,100 vs. $22,400 for #2,” said Newton. “Today it’s $15,200 for #3 and $30,100 for #2.” Accounting for inflation, the average #3 C5 value has gone down from its value 10 years ago, making them a tempting buy for a weekend driver. The split between #3 and #2 cars is a trend that continues with the Z06. The difference between a #2 and #3 Z06 was just $4400 in 2021. Today,[that same good condition Z06](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chevrolet/corvette/2001/2001-chevrolet-corvette-z06?id=aCn1I000000Cu8OSAS) would cost just $2,000 more, yet the[#2 (excellent) example](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chevrolet/corvette/2001/2001-chevrolet-corvette-z06?id=aCn1I000000Cu8OSAS&condition=excellent) would cost $41,800, a $17,000 increase.


Z06s aren’t quite the speed-per-dollar steal that they were in the late 2010s, when really nice ones could be had for under 30 grand, but they are still so much car for the money.


The aftermarket for C5 Corvettes remains strong, and the Gen III GM small-block has picked up the mantle of its predecessors to become the powerplant of choice for hot-rodders. That makes the C5 a popular choice for those looking to maintain their weekend toy as-is, as well as those who’d rather modify their ride. Of course, the market is very clear on which camp can expect to have a better resale value.
